video_title: Trumpism Is Backfiring | The Ezra Klein Show
gist: Former Canadian Deputy PM Chrystia Freeland tells Ezra Klein that Trump's coercive trade policy is backfiring: Canada is retaliating, targeting intermediate-goods and swing-state pain points, and diversifying toward the EU and China ahead of a January US tariff deadline. Allies are cutting dependence on the US (F-35s, Starlink), China is the net winner, and US business capitulation may reverse depending on the midterms.

insights.claim: Canadian PM Mark Carney walked away from trade talks with the Trump administration in late August 2026, and the US and Canada are heading toward a January deadline when massive new US tariffs on Canada take effect.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: January tariff deadline is a dated event risk for cross-border supply chains (autos, aluminum, lumber, potash) and CAD.

insights.claim: A US tariff on Canadian aluminum is effectively a tariff on electricity, because aluminum is 'electricity in solid form' — Quebec smelts it on cheap hydro — so a 50% aluminum tariff raises US input energy costs.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: US aluminum users (packaging, autos, construction) bear the cost; watch US aluminum premiums and downstream margins.
insights.quote: aluminum is basically electricity in solid form. That's all it is.

insights.claim: Freeland says Canada's aluminum exports to the US embody electricity equivalent to more than 450 data centers, or the output of about half a dozen Hoover Dams, linking the tariff to the AI power crunch.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Frames aluminum tariffs as competing with AI data-center power demand; relevant to power-constrained US industrial and AI buildout.
insights.quote: when you put a 50% tariff on aluminum, you're putting a 50% tariff on electricity.

insights.claim: Canada mostly exports intermediate goods to the US (aluminum, softwood lumber, potash for fertilizer), so US tariffs on Canada mainly raise costs for US manufacturers, homebuilders and farmers.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Tariffs on Canada act as input-cost inflation for US housing, agriculture and manufacturing; watch lumber and fertilizer prices.

insights.claim: Canada was the largest export market for the United States, larger than China, Japan and the UK combined, which gives Canadian retaliation real bite despite the size asymmetry.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: US exporters with heavy Canadian exposure are vulnerable to counter-tariffs and boycotts.
insights.quote: But we actually were your biggest market larger than China, Japan, and the UK combined.

insights.claim: Freeland's retaliation playbook: avoid counter-tariffs on intermediate goods, target easily substitutable consumer goods, and aim at products made in swing states and the home states of influential senators so voters feel the pain.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Expect Canadian counter-tariffs to target branded consumer goods from politically sensitive US states; screen consumer companies by state/brand exposure.

insights.claim: In 2018 Canada deliberately targeted Ohio-made Smucker's jam, prompting Senator Sherrod Brown to ask Canada to ease off — which Freeland said was exactly the point.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Precedent that specific US consumer brands get singled out in retaliation; Smucker's-type brands carry political-target risk.

insights.claim: The 2018 dollar-for-dollar Canadian retaliation, joined by the EU and Mexico, ultimately got the US to drop its 232 steel and aluminum tariffs and led to the USMCA deal backed by Trump, Pelosi and Sherrod Brown.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Historical base rate: coordinated retaliation preceded tariff rollback, which supports a scenario of eventual de-escalation.

insights.claim: Freeland's negotiating doctrine with Trump is to neither escalate nor back down, and she argues that flattering him (gifts, outrageous praise) fails because it rests on underestimating him.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Countries that hold firm may get better terms than appeasers; useful for judging which bilateral deals actually stick.
insights.quote: we do not escalate and we do not back down

insights.claim: The Canada-EU CETA agreement is deeper on paper than USMCA because it opens government procurement to each other, giving Canada a ready platform for diversifying away from the US.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Canadian and EU firms may win cross-Atlantic procurement and trade share displaced from US suppliers.

insights.claim: A Canadian poll found 41% of Canadians view the United States as an enemy country, and a Pew poll found more Canadians view China favorably than the US — a reversal from 2023.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Sentiment shift underpins consumer boycotts of US goods/travel and policy pivots away from the US.

insights.claim: Canada is building closer trade ties with China and openly discussing associate membership of the European Union as a hedge against the US, which Freeland says Canadians expected.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Trade diversion away from the US; potential long-term loss of US share in Canadian imports.

insights.claim: Allies are reducing military and tech dependence on the US: countries will hesitate to buy more Pentagon-controlled F-35s, and Europe, Canada and Ukraine are seeking alternatives to Starlink.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Headwind for US defense and space exports; tailwind for European defense and non-US satellite constellations.
insights.quote: countries are going to think really hard before they buy another F-35 controlled by the Pentagon.

insights.claim: Freeland and Klein argue that treating allies as tributaries ('10 times the economy, get our way 10 times as often', per Lighthizer) prompts realist balancing: allies cut short-term deals but coalesce to contain the US long-term.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Erosion of the post-war alliance premium could weigh on the dollar's and US assets' safe-haven status over time.

insights.claim: Trump very arguably elected Carney by threatening Canadian sovereignty, reversing a Conservative surge; Carney walking away from talks has made him the most popular PM in Canadian history.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Canadian political consensus for resisting the US is durable, so don't assume quick Canadian capitulation.

insights.claim: Former Conservative PM Stephen Harper said Canada should pay whatever economic price is needed to defend its sovereignty, showing cross-party consensus for resistance.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: A prolonged standoff is more likely than a quick concession.

insights.claim: Freeland argues most countries initially appeased Liberation Day tariffs, with only China and Canada retaliating, which convinced the Trump team the strategy worked; she calls that a mistake.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Watch for more allies shifting to retaliation, which raises global trade-war escalation risk.

insights.claim: Klein argues no president has done more for China than Trump; Freeland agrees, saying citizens of long-standing US allies now see the US as a bigger threat than an increasingly authoritarian China.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: China's diplomatic and trade position is improving relative to the US; potential tailwind for Chinese exporters into allied markets.

insights.claim: The Democracy Perception Index survey of 98 countries ranked the US fifth-worst perceived, just ahead of Iran and two spots behind Russia, while China was net favorable.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: US soft-power erosion is measurable and could feed into consumer brand boycotts abroad.

insights.claim: Klein's framework: countries value a predictable counterparty even in unequal relationships, and China is a 'predictable predatory hegemon' whereas Trump is erratic, so China wins on reliability.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Policy predictability is a competitive asset; erratic US policy raises the risk premium on US-dependent supply chains.

insights.claim: Freeland argues China broke the global trading system through intentional overcapacity and vicious supply-chain dominance, and that Trump has a point on that issue.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Supports continued allied measures against Chinese overcapacity even while relations with the US sour.
insights.quote: China broke the global trading system through intentional overcapacity and through intentional and pretty vicious building of supply chain dominance.

insights.claim: China coerces through trade: it banned Norwegian salmon over a Nobel Prize, punished Lithuania over Taiwan, and detained two Canadians after Huawei's CFO was arrested.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Exporters to China face retaliation risk tied to their home governments' political choices.

insights.claim: Freeland says China is what an effective Trump administration would seek to become: a predatory, mercantilist hegemon that is good at it.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Frames US policy as aspiring to Chinese-style statecraft; implies more industrial policy and rent-seeking in the US.
insights.quote: China is what an effective Trump administration would seek to become.

insights.claim: Klein argues tariffs are a tool of corruption, enabling a pay-to-play system where the administration rewards friends with favorable merger and contract decisions and punishes enemies.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Regulatory and tariff-exemption outcomes may track political alignment; factor political access into M&A and policy risk.
insights.quote: Tariffs are among other things a tool of corruption.

insights.claim: Klein cites Anthropic: after it tried to limit what its AI would do for the Pentagon, it faced possible designation as a supply-chain risk and exclusion from government contracts, while compliant rivals got contracts.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Government AI contracts may flow to vendors that accept fewer use restrictions; a policy risk for AI firms with usage limits.

insights.claim: Freeland draws on 1990s Russia, where oligarchs got rich by obtaining state assets and installed Putin believing they could control him, as a cautionary tale for US business leaders aligning with Trump.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: A shift from a rules-based market economy to rent-seeking would hurt broad US economic performance even as connected firms benefit.

insights.claim: Klein says Elon Musk put roughly $250 million into trying to save Republicans in the midterms, illustrating how far top business leaders have moved into Trump's coalition compared with the first term.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Business-political alignment raises policy-favoritism risk around companies linked to Musk.

insights.claim: Klein says tech billionaires backed Trump less out of fear of economic populism than out of anger at progressive power centers — media coverage, employee activism, and regulators like Lina Khan.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Tech's political alignment is driven by regulatory and status concerns; antitrust posture is a key variable.

themes.theme: Tipping point and paths to a deal

insights.claim: Freeland predicts a tipping point in business capitulation, dating its start to Jamie Dimon's 28 September Wall Street Journal op-ed calling for a massive US-EU trade and economic deal, which runs opposite to Trump's policies.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Watch for more CEOs publicly backing allied trade; a shift in corporate voice could precede policy reversal.
insights.quote: he called for a massive US EU trade and economic deal.

insights.claim: Freeland believes American business will stay on the side of power, so corporate dissent depends on the midterms: if Trump and MAGA stop delivering at the ballot box, business behavior could change sharply.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Midterm results are the catalyst for a tariff and trade-policy regime shift; position around them.
insights.quote: I think it will depend on the midterms because I think what we've seen from American business is they're going to be on the side of power.

insights.claim: Polling shows Carney's counter-tariffs are more popular with Americans than Trump's tariffs on Canada, and a Michigan Republican Senate candidate ran an ad drinking Labatt and calling to end the tariff war.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Anti-tariff sentiment in swing states raises odds of political pressure for de-escalation before or after the midterms.
insights.quote: Prime Minister Mark Carney's tariff reprisals against Donald Trump are more popular with Americans than Donald Trump's tariffs on Canada are.

insights.claim: Freeland says a deal before January 1 is not required; a negotiation with a ceasefire on further tariffs would suffice, and a plausible deal is an allies-wide pact (Canada, EU, UK) built on a common approach to China.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Expect any de-escalation to come as a tariff standstill plus a China-focused allied framework rather than a quick full deal.
insights.quote: there doesn't have to be a deal before January 1st.

insights.claim: Freeland urges the EU, Mexico, Japan, South Korea and Australia to join Canada in dollar-for-dollar retaliation against US tariffs, and wants the US auto industry to lead business pushback.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Broader allied retaliation would escalate risk for US exporters, while auto-industry lobbying is a lever for relief.

insights.claim: Freeland names the US-launched war in Iran as a war of choice that made Trump less effective, and says CEOs who donated to Trump are now scared by the Iran war, the tilt toward Putin and trade wars.
insights.speaker: Chrystia Freeland
insights.so_what: Geopolitical risk (Iran, Russia-Ukraine) is weighing on business confidence in the administration.
